title: Page 1
summary: Excerpt from a redacted 1960s-era document ('Goldsboro Revisited' / 'How I Learned to Mistrust the H-Bomb') quoting Dr. Ralph Lapp's account of a 1961 B-52 incident near Goldsboro, North Carolina, where a 24-megaton bomb fell into a field without exploding. Five of six interlocking safety mechanisms were triggered by the fall, leaving a single switch preventing detonation. Interspersed redacted transcript fragments dispute the complexity of the safety devices (four switches, one ineffective in the air), call it an accident rather than an incident, and discuss the Defense Department and AEC.

title: Page 2
summary: The text is an OCR-garbled excerpt criticizing a report (Lapp's) on nuclear weapon safety as lacking objectivity and accuracy, with erroneous sources. It states that a single simple low-voltage switch stood between the US and a major catastrophe, noting no new safety analysis of the Goldsboro incident is needed since deMontmollin and Hoagland (1961) covered it. It argues the Mk 39 Mod 2 bomb lacked adequate airborne-alert safety, that a B-52 breakup could release bombs in near-normal fashion, and that the only effective safing device is the ready-safe switch (MC772 Goldsboro, MC1288 Alt 197). A short circuit could arm the bomb and cause a nuclear burst. Footnotes cite SC-DR-81-61 on the Greensboro, North Carolina B-52 crash, note the same conclusion applies to present SAC bombs (B28, B53, B41), and mention Palomares.
